questions.prompt: If a method needs to modify its receiver, which receiver type must it use?
questions.explanation: A value receiver operates on a copy, so changes are lost; a pointer receiver operates on the original and can mutate it.

questions.prompt: How does Go reuse behavior across types without inheritance?

options.text: By embedding one type in another, promoting its fields and methods

questions.explanation: Go composes types by embedding; the embedded type's exported fields and methods are promoted to the outer type.

questions.prompt: By convention, a constructor function is named ____ (using the type name Foo).
questions.explanation: Go has no special constructor syntax; the convention is a function named `NewFoo` (or `New` when the package is named after the type) that returns a ready value.

questions.prompt: Which statements about structs and methods are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A struct's zero value has every field at its own zero value
You can attach methods to any named type, not only structs

questions.explanation: Zero-valued structs are often usable, methods work on any named type, and keyed literals resist field reordering. Go has neither classes nor inheritance.

questions.prompt: Match each choice to when you'd make it.

pairs.right: Method mutates the receiver or the struct is large
Small, read-only method on a small type
Reuse another type's fields and methods
Create a struct clearly and safely

questions.explanation: Receiver choice hinges on mutation and size; embedding provides composition; keyed literals are the safe way to construct.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended consistency rule for a type's receivers?

options.text: If any method needs a pointer receiver, give all methods pointer receivers
Always mix value and pointer receivers evenly
Only the constructor may use a pointer
Receivers must all be value receivers

questions.explanation: Keeping a type's method set uniform (all pointer or all value) avoids subtle method-set and interface-satisfaction surprises.
